Two conditions define waiting and both are in the statement: the state must be staged and the review flag set. maintenance.kb_doc_set_state can clear the flag without changing the state, so a document can leave this list while remaining staged.

The typed maintenance.kb_doc_read operation reads one ingested document's row. The identifier carries no scope, and the row's own scope is returned rather than checked, so a caller holding a number reads whichever scope's document it names. The backend cannot separate a document that is not there from a read that failed -- both are the same failure -- so a zero found flag means either, and the normalized text is not part of the row this returns.

The typed maintenance.kb_doc_regions_for_chunk operation lists where in a PDF a chunk's text sits, so an answer can cite a rectangle on a page. The quote is stored rather than derived, so it is what the extractor saw and not necessarily what the document now says -- a re-ingest that changes the text leaves the old quote until the region is rewritten. The chunk identifier carries no project, so a caller holding one reads whichever project's chunk it names.

The typed maintenance.kb_doc_set_state operation sets a document's state. The update names no current state, so any state moves to any other and nothing records what it was. It does not check that a row matched either, so an identifier that names nothing is acknowledged. The review reason is written only when the review flag is being cleared, so a caller cannot record a reason and leave the flag standing. The stamp is DB2's clock.

The typed maintenance.kb_document_fetch operation reads one indexed document chunk. An empty project is not a missing argument: the identifier is unique across the corpus, so an empty project reads whichever project's document it names and returns that project rather than checking it. The backend's own comment says this is for whole-corpus search. Only the current generation of a project the index calls current is visible, so a project mid-reindex answers as though the document were gone.

The typed maintenance.kb_documents_delete_for_file operation deletes every chunk of a file. The backend returns void, so a delete that matched nothing and one that removed a thousand chunks are the same acknowledgement -- for a destructive operation, that is the reply saying least where it matters most. An empty file path is not refused here, so what it deletes depends entirely on what the backend's statement does with one.

The typed organization.document_stored_hash operation reads the hash recorded for a document. Only the project's current generation answers, so a document indexed under an older generation reads back empty -- the same empty as a path nobody has indexed, and the same as a failed read. A caller using this to decide whether a file changed sees an unchanged file as a new one across a generation bump.

The typed organization.document_hash_exists operation asks whether a project's current generation already holds content with this hash. Two tables are searched and one path comes back, so the sample names one file with that content and never says how many there are, nor which of the two tables it came from. Both halves are scoped to the current generation, so identical content indexed under an older one does not count as present.

The typed maintenance.kb_documents_link_neighbours operation joins a chunk to the one before it. Neither identifier is checked to exist, so a chunk can be linked to a predecessor that is not there, and the backend returns void, so nothing says which happened. The link is written from both sides in separate statements outside a transaction, so a failure between them leaves the two chunks disagreeing about whether they are neighbours.

The typed organization.document_chunk_ids operation lists the chunks a file was split into. Only the project's current generation is listed, so a file indexed under an older one has no chunks as far as this operation is concerned. The list stops at the row bound and says nothing about having stopped, which matters because its caller, the curator invalidation, uses the list to decide what to stale -- a file with more chunks than the bound leaves the rest valid.

The typed maintenance.kb_documents_set_tsr_state operation sets the table-recognition state for every chunk of a file. It is a bulk write with no count: the backend returns void, so a caller learns neither how many chunks moved nor whether the file exists. The state is free text nothing checks, so a misspelling is stored and every reader filtering on the intended value silently skips those chunks.

The typed index.file_index_delete_current_generation operation deletes a project's file index for its current generation only. It is one letter away from index.file_index_delete_project, which deletes every generation, and the names are the only thing telling them apart. The project name goes through a helper called db2_kb_resolve_project which copies it and resolves nothing, so an alias matches no rows. A project with no current generation reports zero, and so does an index that was already empty.

The typed index.file_index_delete_project operation removes a project's file index entries across every generation. The name goes through db2_kb_resolve_project, which despite the name copies the string and does nothing else, so the project is matched exactly and an alias matches nothing. Unlike the document clears it is a single statement with nothing to leave half-done, and it does not check whether that statement finished, so a failure reports zero deleted rather than an error.

The typed maintenance.kb_file_index_get operation reads what the index knows about one ingested file. The project name is resolved through an alias before the lookup, so the name that comes back to a caller is not necessarily the name it sent. Only the current generation of a project whose lifecycle is current matches, so a project being re-indexed answers as though the file were never ingested. A read that fails and a file that is absent are both a zero flag.
The typed lifecycle.health operation exposes canonical KB-table readiness together with the schema probe; that evidence remains DB2 authority.

The typed maintenance.kb_ingest_queue_claim_next operation takes the next ingest job and marks it running. It is the one work-claiming operation in this migration that does it correctly: the row is chosen and updated in a single statement whose subquery locks it and skips rows another worker already holds, so two workers claiming at once get different jobs rather than the same one. Priority orders the queue, then identifier.

The typed maintenance.kb_ingest_queue_complete operation marks an ingest job done and records what it did. The update names no current status, so a job that was never claimed, or one already failed, is marked done just the same and its earlier outcome is overwritten. Nothing checks that a row matched, so a job identifier that names nothing is acknowledged. The three counts are the caller's and nothing verifies them; the completion stamp is DB2's clock.

The typed maintenance.ingest_queue_fail operation replaces the failure write. The completion stamp is DB2's clock, and the statement has no condition on the job's current state, so a job that already succeeded is moved to failed just the same. The backend discards the step result, so the acknowledgement means the statement was prepared and nothing more: a job identifier that matches nothing is acknowledged.

The typed maintenance.kb_ingest_queue_recent operation lists recent ingest jobs, running first and pending next by a CASE the statement carries. So this is not a recency list despite its name: a job running for an hour outranks one that finished a second ago. It carries no job identifier, so a caller cannot follow a particular job across two calls or pair a row here with maintenance.kb_ingest_queue_complete.

The typed maintenance.ingest_queue_reset_running operation replaces the startup recovery that returns queue rows abandoned by a dead worker to the pending pool. The two states and the clearing of started_at are fixed policy. Clearing the claim instant is the part that matters: a row left marked as claimed by a process that no longer exists is work that never runs again, and a caller able to skip the clear would hand back a row that still looks taken.

The typed maintenance.kb_ingest_queue_stats operation counts the ingest queue. The four numbers come from three separate statements outside a transaction -- one grouping, then a count of the day's completions, then of its failures -- so a job finishing between them is counted in one and not the other, and the four need not describe any single moment. The two day counts are windows the backend fixes; the request cannot move them.

The typed organization.pdf_quarantine_confirm operation replaces the confirm. It only touches a pending PDF at the project's current generation, so a stale one, or one already confirmed, counts zero rather than failing -- a caller reading zero as an error would be wrong.

The typed organization.pdf_quarantine_reject operation replaces the reject. It is the mirror of confirm and deletes rather than clears, under the same generation and pending conditions; the count is rows removed.

The typed organization.pdf_tsr_state operation reads a PDF's text-scan state. The statement narrows three ways the arguments do not show: the document must be a PDF, it must be in the project's current generation, and it must not still be awaiting a quarantine decision. A document held in pending quarantine therefore reads back empty, which is also what a document of another kind reads back, and what a missing one reads back.

The typed organization.fence_active operation replaces the fence probe. It composes two runtime-state reads and fails closed: an identity row with no heartbeat reads as active, so a partially written fence is never reported inactive. That rule is the whole point of the probe and is not visible in the Boolean it answers with.

The typed organization.purge_fence_clear operation removes a purge fence. It checks the fence still names this generation and purge before deleting, inside the transaction it holds, so a caller cannot clear someone else's fence. The two rows go in the order identity then timestamp, which is the reverse of how they are written: an interrupted clear leaves an orphan timestamp, which the fence check treats as no fence, so the failure direction is open rather than stuck.

The typed organization.purge_fence_heartbeat operation refreshes a purge fence's timestamp. Unlike the bare advisory guard it uses, this operation opens the transaction, takes the lock, checks the fence still names this generation and purge, writes and commits -- all inside the module -- so it is one of the few purge-route pieces that crosses the boundary intact. A fence naming a different purge is refused, and so is one that has been cleared; the reply cannot tell those from a database error.

The typed maintenance.kb_purge_fence_read operation reports who is purging a project. A fence that exists is not the same as one that is live: the owner heartbeats, and a fence whose heartbeat has aged past a third of its lifetime is stale rather than absent -- so a caller can tell an abandoned purge from no purge and take it over deliberately. The backend's -1 arrives as not-present, which is the one collapse here: a read that failed says the field is clear.

The typed organization.release_add_doc operation replaces the release membership insert. Both ends are foreign keys, so an unknown release or an unknown document is refused and the reply says so -- this is not a write that always succeeds. Adding a document already in the release does nothing and is still acknowledged, so a caller cannot tell a repeat from a first add, which is what makes a retry safe.

The typed organization.release_create operation opens a document release. The name is unique, so a second create with a name already taken is refused and answers zero -- the same zero as any other failure, and the operation gives no way to ask for the identifier the existing release has. Identifiers start at one, so zero never names a release. It pairs with organization.release_add_doc, which takes the identifier this returns.

The typed custody.release_get_active operation reads the pointer to the release the system currently answers as. Zero covers three different situations: no key, a value that does not parse, and a value that is not positive. The parse happens through atoll, which returns zero for garbage without saying so, and the catalog records both collapses rather than letting a zero read as a confident no release.

The typed maintenance.kb_release_promote operation retires the active release, promotes another and points the runtime at it. The target is read first, because db2_kb_release_set_state reports success when its UPDATE matches no row: without that read, promoting a release that did not exist retired the one that did, succeeded, and left the installation with no active release. The three writes are one transaction, so a failure partway leaves the release that was active still active.

The typed maintenance.kb_release_read operation reads one documentation release. The two stamps are separate columns rather than a history, so a release promoted, retired and promoted again carries only the last of each and nothing says which came first. A release that is not there and a read that failed are the same failure, so a zero found flag means either.

The typed maintenance.kb_release_rollback operation promotes a release back. A target of zero means the most recently retired one, found by a separate read before the promote, so a rollback racing another promote can pick a release that stopped being the newest retired one in between. With a target it is maintenance.kb_release_promote and carries what that carries. A rollback with nothing retired to return to is refused.

The typed maintenance.runtime_state_get operation replaces the runtime-state read, and is the first on the described wire format: its request and reply are a schema in the catalog rather than a shape someone wrote codecs for. A key that is not set reads back as the empty value, so a caller cannot tell an unset key from one set to nothing -- which matters because runtime_state_touch writes a stamp and reading nothing back looks the same as never having touched it.

The typed maintenance.runtime_state_set operation replaces the runtime-state write. Unlike runtime_state_touch beside it, the value is the caller's rather than DB2's clock, and an existing key is overwritten rather than refused -- this sets, it does not create.

The typed maintenance.runtime_state_touch operation replaces the timestamp upsert. The value written is DB2's clock rather than anything the caller supplies, so this records that something happened and never when a caller says it did.

The typed custody.vector_rebuild_lock_release operation deletes the rebuild lock row. It does not check who holds it, so any caller can release another's lock; that is recorded rather than implied. It returns void, so like the proposal archive it cannot report a failure and the catalog says so.

The typed custody.vector_rebuild_lock_try_acquire operation claims the vector rebuild lock. It is a check followed by a separate write, so two callers can both observe the lock free and both claim it: it does not provide mutual exclusion. The catalog records that as atomicity check-then-set and mutually_exclusive false so the gap is stated where a reader will find it, rather than inferred from the word lock.

The typed maintenance.kb_async_job_get operation reads one asynchronous job. It returns who claimed it and when, so a stuck job is diagnosable -- but nothing says what a claim expires after, so whether one is stale is the caller's judgement. The attempt count rises on every claim, so a job retried by a worker that keeps dying reads like one genuinely retried that often. Found is 1 here and 0 is no such job, the opposite of most reads in this module.

The one declaration in a DB2 header implemented outside the module: it resolves the host executable and spawns a drain worker, issuing no statement. It must not become a wire operation. A bus caller able to reach it could ask the DB2 module to start a process on the host, which is exactly the authority the module boundary exists to withhold. The declaration belongs in the KB service headers.

The typed maintenance.kb_async_queue_status operation counts the asynchronous job queue. It returns a total as well as the four states, so a caller can tell whether the states account for the queue -- which the other counting operations in this module leave it to guess. The processed figure is not a state but a running tally the drain keeps, so it counts work rather than rows and does not belong in that sum.

The typed organization.clear_current_project operation deletes only the current generation's documents for a project, with the vector index operations that point at them. It differs from clear_project in scope and in one other way worth naming: a failed index-operation delete is fatal here and ignored there. Like its sibling it matches the project name exactly -- db2_kb_resolve_project only copies it -- and runs its two statements without a transaction.

The typed organization.clear_project operation deletes a project's documents and the vector index operations pointing at them. Three things are recorded rather than left in the source: the project name is matched exactly, because db2_kb_resolve_project copies it and resolves nothing the name suggests; the index-operation delete runs first because no foreign key cascades it; and its failure is ignored here while the current-generation variant treats it as fatal.

The typed maintenance.kb_project_status operation counts what a project has ingested. The project name comes back as well as going in, because the backend resolves it through an alias -- so a caller can see which project actually answered. The token count is a sum of a stored per-chunk figure rather than a count of anything, so it is as accurate as whatever wrote it, and an int, so a large corpus overflows where the chunk count would not.

The typed maintenance.kb_reembed_status operation reads how a re-embedding run is going. There is at most one, so no identifier is needed and none is returned -- which also means a caller cannot tell a second run from the same run restarted. Progress is a done count against a total captured when the run began, so memories added since are outside both and the fraction can reach one while work remains.

The typed maintenance.count_embeddings_for_version operation counts indexed memory embeddings. It does not count them for a version. The backend requires the version to be non-empty and then never binds it: the statement counts every memory_units row whose status is ok, and vector_index_ops has no version column to filter on. The argument is on the wire because it is in the declaration, and the replay asks twice with different versions to show the answer does not move.

The typed maintenance.kb_directive_resolve operation resolves a directive. It differs from maintenance.directive_resolve in two ways the identical reply cannot show. It checks openness in one statement and writes in another rather than resolving only an open directive in one, so a directive resolved between the two is resolved again and its earlier resolution overwritten. And the note is discarded: the backend takes it and voids it, so nothing a caller writes there is ever stored.

The same suppression reached through a second header, and the reason it gets no operation of its own. This variant checks that the directive is open in a separate query and then updates without the guard, so the state can change between the two. The boundary binds the variant whose single statement carries the guard, and listing both symbols on one operation keeps the pair from diverging unnoticed.

This is db2_directive_sweep_expired again: the same UPDATE, character for character once whitespace is normalised, reached through a second header. It gets no operation of its own. It joins maintenance.directive_sweep_expired, and because the two disagree about failure -- this one returns -1 where the other returns 0 -- the boundary binds this one, so a failed sweep is reported instead of being read as an empty one.
The cJSON feedback facade is caller-specific presentation; a typed learning mutation validates bounded polarity, title, description, and weight.

The typed maintenance.active_embedder_version operation reads which embedder version is active. There is one row to read, so an empty answer means no embedder has ever been made active, and is also what a failed read gives. It pairs with maintenance.set_active_embedder_version, and a caller comparing the two is comparing against DB2's record rather than against whatever its own process was built to run.

The typed memory.memory_ids_by_updated operation lists memories newest-updated first. Every tier is included, unlike the other memory listings beside it, and a caller cannot tell a list cut at the bound from one that ended.

The typed maintenance.reembed_mark_finished operation replaces the completion stamp. The caller supplies the stamp here, unlike the other writes in this family, because it is recording when a run it watched ended.

The unused-L2 cJSON report stays local serialization; a typed query bounds age and result rows and returns explicit truncation.
The evaluation-corpus cJSON document is caller presentation; a typed bounded query returns labeled memory records and truncation state.
The cJSON maintenance report cannot define the work boundary; a typed operation owns the complete maintenance run and returns bounded counters.
The prospective-complete cJSON wrapper is local presentation; a typed mutation validates the transition and returns explicit status.
The prospective-create cJSON facade is not the mutation contract; a typed operation bounds all fields and returns the new identifier and result.
The prospective-memory cJSON list is caller rendering; a typed bounded query returns prospective records and truncation evidence.
The trigger-state cJSON wrapper remains local presentation; a typed mutation owns the state change and returns explicit affected state.
The prospective-match cJSON response is compatibility rendering; a typed request bounds the observation and returns structured matches.
The expiry-sweep cJSON report stays local presentation; a typed maintenance mutation owns the sweep and returns bounded counts.
The graph-edge cJSON response is caller rendering; a typed bounded query returns canonical edge records and truncation state.
The memory-health cJSON document is presentation-only; typed bounded counters and diagnostic flags define the operation reply.
The recall cJSON envelope remains local serialization; a typed request bounds query and scope fields and returns structured recall records.

The typed memory.record_exists operation replaces the record probe. It consults two tables -- memories and memory_units -- and the reply says only that one of them matched, not which, so a caller cannot use it to tell a memory identifier from a unit identifier. That is deliberate and is written into the policy, because the wire cannot show it.
The memory-reject cJSON wrapper is not the state-transition contract; a typed mutation validates the reason and returns explicit status.
The conversation-scan cJSON input and report are compatibility presentation; a typed operation validates bounded directories and returns structured counts.
The scope-rank cJSON object is caller presentation; a typed bounded request returns explicit visibility and rank fields.
The keyword-search cJSON array is local rendering; a typed request bounds the keyword and returns bounded fact and pattern records.
The temporal graph-search cJSON response is presentation-only; a typed operation validates the timestamp and returns bounded relation records.
The graph-search cJSON document remains caller serialization; typed bounded query fields and relation records define the stable reply.
The general search cJSON response cannot cross the typed ABI; a bounded operation returns structured matches and explicit truncation.
The artifact-update cJSON facade is not the mutation contract; a typed operation validates bounded artifact fields and returns explicit status.
The memory-stat cJSON response is compatibility rendering; fixed typed counters and scores form the stable operation reply.
The supersede cJSON wrapper cannot define or split the transaction; a typed memory.supersede operation owns version closure, replacement insert, provenance, and result.
The scope-tag cJSON facade remains local presentation; a typed mutation validates the closed scope type and bounded value.
The workspace-tag cJSON wrapper is not the mutation ABI; a typed operation bounds the workspace and returns explicit status.
The top-L2 cJSON array is caller rendering; a typed bounded query returns ranked fact records and truncation state.
The touch cJSON wrapper remains local presentation; a typed idempotent mutation owns usage updates and returns explicit found state.
The memory-update cJSON facade is not the mutation contract; a typed operation validates bounded content and returns structured update status.
The workflow-upsert cJSON response is compatibility presentation; a typed composite operation bounds workflow fields and owns the complete upsert.
The cJSON note-creation wrapper is caller presentation code; a typed learning mutation bounds note fields and returns an explicit identifier and result.
The cJSON note-list builder stays local; a typed learning operation returns a bounded tag-filtered record set.
The cJSON note-search response cannot define the wire shape; DB2 returns bounded typed matches for caller-owned serialization.
The relation-schema cJSON list is caller presentation; a typed bounded query returns canonical relation definitions and truncation state.

The typed maintenance.reset_stuck_vector_ops operation replaces the stuck-op reset. It resets two separate queues -- the memory and evidence vector ops, and the code-chunk ops -- and adds their counts, so a caller cannot tell which queue the rows came from. Worse, each half reports a negative on failure, so one failing while the other succeeds produces a smaller number rather than an error. That is the backend's arithmetic and is recorded here because the count looks ordinary.
The cJSON decay report is presentation-only; one typed learning maintenance operation owns decay and returns bounded aggregate evidence.
The cJSON delete facade is not transported; a typed learning mutation owns rule deletion and returns its closed result.
The cJSON filesystem-export wrapper is process-local orchestration; a bounded export operation owns the path policy and returns typed counts.
The cJSON generation report remains local presentation; a typed learning operation performs generation and returns bounded counts.
The cJSON insert wrapper is caller serialization; a typed mutation validates bounded polarity, title, description, and weight before persistence.
The cJSON rule-list builder cannot cross the stable bus; DB2 returns a bounded typed rule record set.
The cJSON directive-type update is a legacy facade; a typed learning mutation validates the closed type and returns structured status.
The cJSON scene-list facade is process-local presentation code; the existing fixed scene rows define a bounded memory operation reply instead.
The cJSON scene-member facade stays out of the transport contract; DB2 returns a bounded array of fixed member records and the caller renders JSON.
The session-commitment cJSON array remains local rendering; a typed bounded briefing query returns commitment records.
The session-directive cJSON array is caller presentation; a typed bounded briefing query returns directive records.

The typed maintenance.set_active_embedder_version operation replaces the version write. It targets one fixed row, so this switches the active version rather than adding one, and the stamp is the caller's. What it does not do is check that the version has any embeddings; the count that was supposed to gate that is recorded as broken at db2_kb_service_count_embeddings_for_version.
The cJSON edge-mutation wrapper is caller presentation code; a typed learning operation validates task identifiers and the closed relation before persistence.
The cJSON task-creation facade is not transported; a typed mutation bounds title, session, and parent and returns an explicit identifier and result.
The cJSON task-delete wrapper stays outside the wire shape; DB2 performs the typed mutation and returns a closed result.
The cJSON edge-list response remains local serialization; a typed operation returns a bounded task-edge record set.
The cJSON task-list builder cannot define the stable contract; DB2 returns bounded state- and session-filtered task records.
The cJSON task-state facade is retired at the process boundary; a typed mutation validates the closed state and returns structured status.
The tool-lookup cJSON object remains a compatibility facade; a typed bounded name request returns the registry record and explicit found state.
The tool-registry snapshot cJSON tree cannot cross the typed module ABI; a bounded typed snapshot operation owns records and truncation evidence.
Beginning a caller-held content transaction cannot cross the module boundary; each document, PDF, or code-index mutation becomes one bounded operation with DB2-owned atomicity.
Caller-controlled content commits are private DB2 mechanics; a complete index-family mutation commits before returning its structured reply and never exposes a transaction token.
Content transaction rollback stays inside DB2; failed, denied, or cancelled composite index operations roll back before returning and cannot leave caller-owned database state.

Per-kind promotion, demotion, and expiry thresholds are a private input to the tier-cycle operations that apply them; exposing the lookup alone would let a caller act on thresholds DB2 had already superseded.

The typed learning.commits_in_last_7_days operation replaces the recent-commit count. The seven-day window and the clock it is measured against are both DB2's and never cross, so a caller cannot widen the window or supply its own now; the count is only meaningful beside that fact.

The typed learning.proposal_archive operation archives a learning proposal and records why. The update names no current state, so a proposal already committed is archived too and the commitment is lost from the state column. Nothing checks that a row matched, so archiving a proposal that does not exist is acknowledged. An empty reason is accepted and stored as one, so a proposal can be archived with nothing saying why.

The typed learning.proposal_bump_corroboration operation replaces the corroboration bump. The count is incremented by the statement rather than supplied, so a caller records that a proposal was corroborated again without being able to set or read the total. Only a pending proposal is bumped, but the acknowledgement reports that the statement ran and not that a row matched, so corroborating a committed proposal -- or one that does not exist -- does nothing and says it succeeded.

The typed learning.proposal_find_pending operation finds whether a target already has a proposal waiting, so a caller can avoid raising a second. It takes the newest of them, which means duplicates can exist and this only ever reveals one -- it prevents a third rather than the second. All three of sink, key and memory must match exactly, so a proposal about the same thing recorded under a different key is invisible to the check.

The typed learning.proposal_get operation reads one learning proposal. The action it proposes is JSON the writer assembled, so what a proposal would do is text this boundary carries without understanding -- a caller deciding whether to commit one is parsing the writer's words. The expiry is a stamp with no enforcement here, so an expired proposal reads exactly like a live one and only the caller comparing it to a clock can tell.

The typed learning.proposal_insert operation raises a proposal. Its two references are not treated alike: the signal it cites carries a foreign key, so citing one that does not exist is refused by the database, while the memory it targets carries none and may name anything. Nothing prevents a duplicate -- learning.proposal_find_pending exists so a caller can check first, which makes that the caller's discipline rather than the table's.

The typed learning.proposal_mark_committed operation replaces the commit write. Unlike the corroboration bump beside it there is no condition on the proposal's state, so committing one that was already committed overwrites its commit stamp with a later one -- which matters to anything reading when a proposal landed. Both stamps are DB2's clock.

The typed learning.proposals_archive_expired operation replaces the sweep that archives learning proposals past their expiry. The states, the archive reason and the database clock are fixed policy. This backend returns void and logs its failures, so the boundary cannot report one either; the catalog records reports_failure as false rather than letting an always-ok acknowledgement imply a guarantee that is not there.

The typed learning.proposals_settled_counts operation counts learning proposals that settled inside a window. The two counts are not disjoint: terminal counts committed and archived together, so every committed proposal is in both and a caller subtracting one from the other gets the archived count rather than a remainder. A proposal falls in the window by whichever of its committed, updated or created stamps exists, so an old proposal touched recently counts as settled recently.
Lease scope terminates process-local PostgreSQL ownership and has no wire representation; it disappears when the enclosing DB2 work becomes one bounded request.
Idle-lease release is process-local pool hygiene, not a remote database operation; the standalone owner releases its own leases between complete bus requests.

Applying transaction-local PostgreSQL maintenance context is private DB2 execution state; each maintenance wire operation carries its bounded worker and project scope and owns the complete transaction.
The thread-local maintenance job binding cannot cross a process boundary; generated operations carry the named worker and bounded project on every complete DB2 request.
Clearing a process-local maintenance job binding has no wire representation; explicit request scope replaces the caller-owned thread-local lifetime.
Beginning a PostgreSQL transaction from thread-local maintenance state is private DB2 execution; a typed operation validates explicit scope and begins its own transaction instead.
A caller-controlled commit is forbidden across the module boundary; each declared maintenance mutation commits before publishing its bounded reply.
A caller-controlled rollback is process-local transaction cleanup; failed or cancelled maintenance operations roll back inside DB2 before returning transport status.

The same shape for a management action: bounds-checks every field, hex-renders the request digest, and mints the correlation id and jti the intent will carry. Caller-side argument construction, reaching no store. The identifiers it generates are what make the intent it precedes idempotent, so generating them at the caller is deliberate.

Packs an issuer, a subject and two anchors into a client-instance binding and computes the digest over them. The digest is the identity of the binding, so computing it beside the values rather than after they have crossed a wire is what keeps it a digest of what the caller meant. It reaches no store.

The typed memory.dedupe_candidates operation lists the active memories of one kind so a caller can find duplicates among them. It returns the fields a caller would use to choose which duplicate to keep -- confidence, uses, observations, evidence -- and no content, so the comparison this feeds is over keys and scores rather than over what the memories say. The kind is matched exactly, so a caller must know the vocabulary the writers used.

The typed memory.aggregate operation replaces the aggregation read. Three statements hide behind it, chosen by which argument is set: an entity seed wins outright, the keyword is consulted only when the seed is empty, and neither selects every kind but scratch. That precedence is invisible to a caller sending both. It over-fetches by one row to learn whether it truncated and reports that separately, because a full list and a truncated one look the same. Identifiers cross; it is unscoped.

The typed memory.alias_insert operation records another name for a memory. The backend returns void, so the acknowledgement says the call was made and can never say the row landed. Nothing deduplicates the alias, so the same name recorded twice is two rows and a reader counting aliases counts calls. The weight is stored as sent and nothing bounds it.

Private first half of memory_refresh_aliases: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.briefing_active_entities operation ranks the entities mentioned by recently touched memories. The window is roughly the last month, and a memory with no last-used stamp counts as recent rather than as old, so a freshly written memory that has never been read still ranks. The ordering leads with the newest memory identifier rather than the mention count, so one new memory can move an entity above a more mentioned one.

The typed memory.briefing_key_facts operation lists the facts a session briefing opens with. Only the durable tiers are listed -- L2 through L5 -- so a fact still in a session tier is absent however important it is. The ordering is a scope-rank expression the statement carries, then confidence, so what reaches a briefing is decided by that expression and a caller cannot ask for a different order. Its caller asks for one row, which makes the ordering the whole answer.

The typed memory.briefing_recent_activity operation lists what happened recently, one episode a session. The one is chosen by a window function inside the statement, which the query's own comment says exists so a limit cannot eliminate an older active-project session before the ranking runs -- so the row a session contributes is decided there, not by recency. The reference time is a text column separate from the created stamp, so an episode can be about a time other than when it was written.

Private second half of memory_refresh_chunks: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

Private lookup inside the chunk rebuild: the value is read only to feed the rows that same rebuild is about to write, and is never returned to a caller. Exposing it would publish an intermediate of a composite operation as though it were an answer in its own right.

The typed memory.collect_alias_matches operation replaces the alias probe. The three ways an alias can match and the order they rank in are DB2's, computed in one statement against the alias table, so they stay behind the handler. It returns identifiers rather than rows for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.collect_entity_matches operation replaces the entity probe. Exact, prefix and substring matches all come back from one statement and rank in that order, which the caller cannot reconstruct from a plain list. It returns identifiers rather than rows for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.collect_event_frame_matches operation replaces the frame probe. One term is tried against the actor, the action, the location and the event time exactly and against the object as a substring; which field matched does not reach the caller and does not change the order. It returns identifiers rather than rows for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.collect_relation_token_matches operation replaces the relation probe. A memory can match through several relations, so the statement groups by memory and ranks on the greatest matching weight; that collapse is DB2's and stays behind the handler. It returns identifiers rather than rows for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.collect_summary_matches operation replaces the summary probe. The match is a case-insensitive substring and a prefix outranks the rest, which is policy the caller does not choose. It returns identifiers rather than rows for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.collect_temporal_matches operation replaces the temporal probe. Only exact and prefix reference keys match -- there is no substring arm here, unlike the alias and entity probes -- and exact outranks prefix. It returns identifiers rather than rows for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.
Fetching conflict member IDs is a private read inside the future memory.conflict_resolve transaction; the pair must remain stable through conflict update, audit logging, and directive closure.

The typed memory.conflict_list operation lists contradictions between memories, newest first. Only unresolved ones are listed and that filter is in the statement rather than the request, so a caller cannot ask what was resolved or how -- which makes the resolved and resolution columns it returns constant: the first is always zero and the second always empty. There is no scope: this is every unresolved conflict the installation holds.
Creating the conflict row is one private step of the future memory.conflict_record transaction, which must also create its audit, relationship, and directive evidence before replying.

Updating a conflict row is a private step of the future memory.conflict_resolve transaction; exposing it alone would allow the audit log and contradiction directive to disagree with canonical conflict state.
Contradiction audit insertion is private evidence written by complete conflict record and resolve operations; a standalone best-effort wire mutation could diverge from the conflict row it documents.

The typed memory.coref_audit_insert operation records how a coreference was resolved. It is an audit row whose write cannot be confirmed: the backend returns void, so the acknowledgement says the call was made. An audit trail that cannot report its own failure is the one place that matters most, and this one shares the shape with every other void writer here rather than being singled out.
The typed memory.total_count operation replaces the read-only global corpus count while preserving the legacy 64-bit result width; canonical relational memory rows remain DB2 authority.

The typed memory.count_and_max_updated operation replaces the aggregate that fingerprints the memory corpus. The stamp is empty for an empty corpus, which is a real answer rather than an absent one, so the reply carries a zero-minimum string alongside the count and reserves invalid_state for an aggregate that could not be computed.

The typed memory.tier_kind_counts operation counts memories by tier and kind. Unlike the other counting operations here it names no states of its own -- it returns whatever pairs the column holds -- so nothing is dropped and the counts do add up to the table. That also means a misspelt tier or kind appears as its own row rather than vanishing, which is the property the state-counting operations lack.
The typed memory.level2_count operation replaces the bounded global working-memory count; canonical relational memory rows remain DB2 authority.
The typed memory.session_l2_count operation replaces the bounded per-session retention probe; canonical session attribution and L2 rows remain DB2 authority.
The typed memory.level3_count operation replaces the bounded global corpus-count query; canonical relational memory rows remain DB2 authority.
The typed memory.orphaned_l0_count operation replaces the bounded integrity diagnostic for unlinked short-term memories; canonical relational links remain DB2 authority.

Counting version suffixes is private read-modify-write state for the future composite memory.supersede operation; exposing the count separately would race concurrent supersedes and split one logical DB2 mutation.

The typed memory.decay_confidence operation replaces the unconditional confidence decay; the multiplier stays fixed policy behind the handler. The backend returns void and so cannot report whether the row existed, which the acknowledgement-only reply preserves rather than inventing a count.

The typed memory.dedupe_by_key operation replaces the deduplication pass. The flag decides whether it writes: a dry run counts the memories it would merge and changes nothing, so the same number means two entirely different things and a caller that loses track of which it asked for cannot recover it from the reply. Merging keeps the highest-confidence memory for each key and points the rest at it.

The typed memory.delete_row operation replaces the canonical row delete and reports whether the named memory existed; the row is DB2 authority and any derived vector removal is a separate provider concern.

Private first half of the entity refresh: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.entities_list operation lists the entities a memory mentions, heaviest first. The weight is returned, so a caller can see where it was cut off -- unlike most lists here, truncation is legible. Its callers ask for sixteen, which the reply carries many times over, so the cut is the caller's array rather than the wire.

The typed memory.entity_insert operation records that a memory mentions an entity in a role. The backend returns void, so the acknowledgement cannot say the row landed. The same entity in the same role recorded twice is two rows, which memory.entities_list then returns as two -- so a caller ranking by weight sees the same entity twice at the same weight rather than once.

Private second half of memory_refresh_episode_relations: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

Private lookup inside the episode rebuild: the value is read only to feed the rows that same rebuild is about to write, and is never returned to a caller. Exposing it would publish an intermediate of a composite operation as though it were an answer in its own right.
