The typed memory.episodes_search operation searches episodes by substring. An empty query is not an empty result: the statement tests for it explicitly and matches everything, so a caller that forgot to fill the query reads the whole corpus rather than nothing. A non-empty query is wrapped in wildcards on both sides, so it matches anywhere in the text and a query containing a LIKE metacharacter matches more than its own words.

Private second half of the event-frame refresh: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

Private first half of the event-frame refresh: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.event_frames_list operation lists the event frames extracted from a memory. The event time is a free-text column rather than a stamp, so it holds whatever the extractor wrote -- a date, a phrase, or nothing -- and two frames cannot be ordered by when they happened, only by when they were written. Every field is optional and an absent one is an empty string, so a frame with no actor and one with an empty actor are the same row.
Releasing process-owned export buffers is local lifetime management; the memory export operation encodes bounded rows into its reply and frees every allocation before returning.

The typed memory.fact_history operation replaces the version walk. The caller sends the normalised key; forming the versioned keys from it is the handler's, so the naming convention does not become a caller's business. It is unscoped, unlike every other search here -- a fact's history is its history whatever the session. Its statement has no LIMIT: the database returns every version and the limit only decides how many are read back, which is a cost the wire cannot show and so is recorded in the policy.

The typed memory.conflicting_l2 operation finds a confident memory that disagrees with what a caller is about to write. Disagreement is a byte comparison, so the same statement with different spacing conflicts with itself. The confidence threshold of four fifths is written into the statement rather than passed, so a caller cannot ask a different question. One conflicting memory is returned of however many there are, and which one is not decided by anything.

The typed memory.find_facts_like operation replaces the fact search. One term is matched case-insensitively against the key, the content and the use cases, and the five-way ranking that decides which of those wins is DB2's; a caller given a plain list could not reconstruct it. It returns identifiers for the reason top_l2_facts records, and the session scope travels in the request because the backend reads it from a thread-local that does not follow a call into another process.
The typed memory.find_id_by_key_kind operation replaces the presentation-only lookup with bounded canonical key and kind fields plus explicit found state and identifier.

The typed memory.get operation replaces the row read. It is the first whose reply carries a whole memory row: a caller holding an identifier has nothing else to reattach it to, and one row is about four kilobytes at its widest against the sixteen l2_memory_ids already puts on a caller's stack. The backend answers -1 both for an absent row and for a statement that did not run, so the operation reports not_found for both; that conflation is the backend's. A null provenance category reads back as user_stated.

The typed memory.get_by_unit_id operation resolves a unit to its memory and shares memory.get's row format. It does not fill the same row: its statement asks for eleven columns, so salience, provenance_category and use_cases come back empty rather than absent, and a caller cannot tell an unread column from a genuinely empty one. That is why each operation's policy lists the columns it actually reads. It conflates an absent row with a failed statement the same way memory.get does.

The typed memory.confidence_by_key operation reads the confidence of the memory holding a key. The key column carries no unique constraint and the statement has neither an ordering nor a limit, so a key held by several memories answers with whichever row the database returns first and never says there was a choice. A key nobody holds and a database that could not be reached are both a zero flag.

The typed memory.get_content operation replaces the canonical text read and is the companion to memory.update_content. A missing memory is reported as not_found rather than as empty content, because a stored row may legitimately hold an empty string and the two answers are different.

The typed memory.evidence_fields operation reads a memory's evidence strength and observation count. The count is stored as a sixty-four bit column and read back through an int, so a memory observed more times than an int holds comes back wrapped rather than clamped. A memory that is not there and a database that could not be reached are both a zero flag; the identifier carries no scope.

The typed memory.salience operation reads a memory's salience, answering the caller's own default when there is nothing to read. That default covers three different things -- no such memory, a database it could not reach, and a memory whose salience happens to equal it -- and the reply has no way to tell them apart because the backend does not either. Nothing bounds salience in the schema, so the wire's bound is the first one it has.

Private lookup inside the unit-graph rebuild: the value is read only to feed the rows that same rebuild is about to write, and is never returned to a caller. Exposing it would publish an intermediate of a composite operation as though it were an answer in its own right.

The typed memory.get_source_session operation replaces the session read and is the companion to memory.set_source_session. The backend succeeds only for a non-empty session and reports an absent memory and a blank column identically, so the wire reply is non-empty on ok and everything else is not_found rather than inventing a distinction the backend cannot make.

The typed memory.state_fields operation reads whether a memory has an end date and how often it has been observed and used. The end date is collapsed to a yes or no before it leaves the backend, so a caller cannot learn when -- only that there is one. Both counts are sixty-four bit columns read back through an int. A memory that is not there and a database that could not be reached are both a zero flag.

The typed memory.surprise operation reads a memory's surprise, answering the caller's own default when there is nothing to read. It is memory.salience against a different column and carries the same thing: the default covers a missing memory, an unreachable database and a stored value that happens to match, and nothing distinguishes them. Nothing bounds surprise in the schema, so the wire's bound is the first one it has.

The typed memory.has_workspace_tag operation replaces the existence probe over workspace attribution rows, preserving its hit-or-miss result; the join stays DB2 authority and no workspace identity crosses the bus.

The typed memory.has_scope_type operation replaces the existence probe over scope attribution rows, preserving its hit-or-miss result; the caller names the scope kind and learns only whether one exists, never which scope value.
The typed memory.effectiveness_update operation carries the positive memory identifier and explicit clear state while DB2 owns the canonical nullable column update.

Counting canonical rows for a health-cycle insert is private DB2 bookkeeping; the complete health-record operation owns this pre-step, while independent callers use the existing typed memory.total_count operation.
Counting recent canonical conflicts is a private input to the complete memory health-record operation; its day window and insert remain owned by one DB2 action.
The typed memory.retention_enforce operation applies the complete fixed restricted and sensitive retention policy while DB2 owns deletion of canonical relational memory rows.
The typed memory.effectiveness_demote operation applies the fixed host effectiveness threshold while DB2 owns the canonical relational tier update.
The typed memory.effectiveness_stats operation returns the aggregate effectiveness summary under the fixed host low-effectiveness threshold while DB2 owns the canonical relational memory corpus.
The typed memory.l2_memory_ids operation hands the bounded L2 identifier set across the boundary so the host can join it against DB1 surfacing evidence while DB2 keeps the canonical relational tier.

The typed memory.health_retention operation applies the complete fixed snapshot and contradiction retention policy in one action, so neither half is reachable alone and no partially pruned state is exposed across the bus.
The typed memory.health_retention operation runs contradiction pruning together with health-snapshot pruning under one fixed policy, so this half is never invoked on its own.
The typed memory.health_counters operation returns the complete rolling-window aggregate under the fixed host promotion policy; DB2 owns every count and the host derives only ratios from them.

The typed memory.health_record operation carries only the three host-observed cycle counters; DB2 owns the corpus total and the fixed one-day conflict window it inserts alongside them. The backend returns nothing and discards its step result, so the reply says the call was made and can never say the row landed.
The typed memory.effectiveness_update operation preserves the host-computed binary64 value while DB2 owns the canonical effectiveness column update.
The typed memory.key_exists operation replaces the bounded exact-key probe while preserving explicit backend-error handling; canonical memory keys remain DB2 authority.
The typed memory.key_exists_in_tier_pair operation replaces the bounded canonical-key and tier-pair probe while preserving its Boolean hit-or-miss result.

The typed memory.l1_session_clusters operation counts session-tier memories per session, leaving out one session the caller names -- which is how a caller excludes its own. An empty exclusion excludes nothing, so the natural way to ask for all of them is to send nothing, and memories whose session is empty are excluded by the statement regardless. A session that recorded nothing is absent rather than zero.

The typed memory.session_content operation lists what one session recorded, oldest first. The statement carries no limit -- the caller's array is the only bound, and its caller asks for two hundred and fifty-six -- so a session that recorded more is read in part with nothing saying so. It returns content alone, so two identical contents from the same session are two indistinguishable rows and a caller cannot tell which memory either came from.

The typed memory.session_created_at operation lists when one session's memories were written, oldest first. It is memory.session_content over the same rows in the same order with a different column, so a caller wanting both makes two round trips and must trust that nothing changed between them -- the two answers are only aligned if the session was quiet. Neither carries an identifier that would let a caller pair them.

The typed memory.l2_cross_key_pairs operation finds L2 memories that mention each other's key prefix. It joins the tier against itself and compares with a substring match, so the work is quadratic in how many L2 memories exist and no index helps. The key prefix is taken up to the first underscore, so a key without one is compared whole and a short prefix matches widely.

The typed memory.l2_fact_decision_pairs operation finds facts and decisions that mention each other. Like memory.l2_cross_key_pairs it is a self-join with a substring comparison, so its cost is the product of the two sets and no index helps -- but the two draw from different tiers, so a fact and a decision at the same tier are never paired. Both sides need a confidence above a half.

The typed memory.last_retro_scan operation reads when the retroactive contradiction scan last ran. It finds that by taking the newest contradiction-log row whose free-text details column is exactly 'retroactive_scan', so anything else written into that column with that value moves the answer and a scan recorded with different wording is invisible. There is no scope: this is the whole log. An empty answer means no scan, or a read that failed.

The typed memory.lifecycle_counts operation counts memories by lifecycle state. It names five states and drops every other group, so the five need not add up to the table. The empty state is one of the groups dropped, and memory.lifecycle_get_state answers that same empty column as active -- so a memory can be active to one operation and counted nowhere by the other. There is no scope: this is every memory the installation holds.

The typed memory.lifecycle_get_state operation reads one memory's lifecycle state. An empty column is answered as active, so a memory whose state was never written reads exactly like one that is active -- and memory.lifecycle_counts, which groups by the same column, counts that memory under no state at all. The two operations disagree about the same row. A memory that is not there and a read that failed are both an empty answer.

The typed memory.lifecycle_newly_superseded operation lists memories recently superseded. An empty since is not the beginning of time: the backend substitutes seven days, so a caller asking without a bound gets a week rather than everything, and cannot ask for everything at all. Superseded-at is the row's updated stamp rather than a supersession stamp, so any later edit to a superseded memory moves it back into this window.

The typed memory.lifecycle_stale_pending operation lists pending memories past their deadline. A pending memory whose deadline is empty is absent -- memory.lifecycle_mark_pending always writes one, but memory.lifecycle_update_state can move a memory to pending without one, so the two writers disagree about whether a pending memory has a deadline and this list only sees the half that does. The ordering puts a scope expression ahead of age, so the oldest is not necessarily first.

The typed memory.lifecycle_unresolved_contradictions operation lists contradictions with the text of both sides, so a reader can judge them without a second read. Only the first memory's key is returned, not the second's -- so the two sides are not symmetric in what a caller can see, and identifying the second requires another read. It is the third operation here that lists unresolved contradictions, alongside memory.conflict_list and the directive counts, each returning a different shape of the same rows.

The typed memory.lifecycle_mark_pending operation marks a memory pending and gives it a deadline. The update names no current state, so an archived or superseded memory becomes pending again. Nothing checks that a row matched, so a memory identifier that names nothing is acknowledged. The day count is written into the statement text rather than bound -- it is an integer, so it cannot carry anything else, and the wire keeps it inside a century.

The typed memory.lifecycle_sweep_expired operation replaces the pending time-to-live archival pass; the source state, target state, and archive reason stay fixed policy behind the handler so no caller can archive a different set of rows.

The typed memory.lifecycle_update_state operation moves a memory to a lifecycle state. The state is stored as sent and nothing checks it against a vocabulary, so a misspelling becomes a state that memory.lifecycle_counts counts nowhere and memory.lifecycle_get_state reports back unchanged. Entering superseded or archived closes the memory's event-time interval, but only when it is still open, so a caller who knew the real end date keeps it. The update names no current state.

The typed memory.lineage_insert operation records where an object came from. The object type is free text and the identifier is not checked against anything, so a lineage entry can name an object of a type nothing writes, or one that was deleted, and read back the same as a sound one. It answers with the new identifier, so unlike most writes here a caller can tell the row landed.

The typed memory.memory_link_create operation links one memory to another. The link is directional and the relation is stored without being checked against anything, so a caller can record a relationship no reader understands. Creating a link that already exists does nothing and is acknowledged, so a repeat is indistinguishable from a first -- which is what makes it safe to retry.
The typed memory.link_delete operation replaces the single relation delete; the link identity is the caller's only input and the relation graph stays DB2 authority.

Private lookup inside the episode-relation rebuild: the value is read only to feed the rows that same rebuild is about to write, and is never returned to a caller. Exposing it would publish an intermediate of a composite operation as though it were an answer in its own right.

The typed memory.list_rows operation replaces the tier and kind listing. It is the only read here whose statement is assembled: the tier and kind clauses appear only when their value is non-empty, so an empty value is no filter on that column rather than a match against the empty string, and this is four statements sharing one name. Its LIMIT was interpolated from an unbounded caller integer and is a bounded field on the wire. Identifiers cross and the scope travels, as for the other scoped reads.

The typed memory.artifact_hashed_list operation lists memories carrying an artifact hash. The statement has no ordering, so which memories a truncated answer holds is not decided by anything -- and its caller asks for fifty, which for an installation with more than fifty such memories means fifty arbitrary ones. The hash is what a caller would use to detect a changed artifact, so the ones it does not receive are the ones it cannot check.

The typed memory.memories_by_key operation lists the memories stored under a key. A key is not unique, so several memories may share one, and nothing orders the result -- which of them survives the row bound is whatever the database returned first. No tier or lifecycle condition applies, so an archived memory is listed beside a live one.

The typed memory.memory_candidates operation loads the memories a scorer will rank. The filter picks one of two tier sets and neither contains the other -- the primary set excludes L0 and the fallback excludes L3 and L5 -- so falling back is not widening the search, it is looking somewhere else. The ordering leads with the identifier, so confidence and use count only break ties.

The typed memory.depends_on_keys operation lists the keys a memory declares it depends on. A key is text a writer chose, and nothing checks that a memory holding it exists -- so a dependency on a key nobody wrote reads exactly like one on a key that was deleted, and this cannot tell a caller which. The keys come back as stored, at the column's full width.

The typed memory.global_constraints operation lists the preferences and policies that constrain everything. It leads its ordering with the memory identifier, so the newest constraint comes first and confidence only breaks ties -- a recent low-confidence preference outranks a long-standing high-confidence one. L0 is excluded, so a constraint still in the scratch tier does not constrain anything.

The typed memory.id_key_content operation lists memories newest-updated first. The limit is not a bound but a switch: the statement text carries a LIMIT clause only when the limit is positive, so asking for zero asks for every memory the installation holds. That is the opposite of what zero means everywhere else here, and it is the difference between a bounded read and an unbounded one.

The typed memory.key_facts_provenance operation lists durable facts and preferences with where each came from. The provenance is a sentence the statement assembles -- an action and a session joined by the word 'during' -- so a caller reading it is reading prose composed in SQL rather than fields it can separate. Both it and the supersede date are correlated subqueries evaluated a row at a time, so the cost grows with the limit rather than with the result.

The typed memory.kv_section operation fetches one of five fixed context sections. The section is a number selecting a statement, not a filter, so the five differ in tier, kind and order in ways the reply cannot show -- and a caller has to know which number means which section. The bound admits one to five, so a mistaken number is refused at the boundary rather than reading nothing inside.

The typed memory.low_effectiveness operation lists the memories scoring below a threshold, worst first. A memory whose effectiveness was never scored is null rather than zero and the statement requires a value, so it is absent from this list entirely -- an unscored memory and a well-performing one are equally invisible here, and the two are not the same thing. The tier column is four bytes wide, so a tier name longer than three characters is truncated before the wire sees it.

The typed memory.prior_in_session operation lists what a session recorded before a given memory, newest first. Before means a lower identifier rather than an earlier stamp, which is the same thing only while identifiers are assigned in order -- and nothing here guarantees that across a restore or a merge. The tier is not filtered, unlike the other session reads here, so this one sees every tier and they see one.

The typed memory.recall_section operation fetches one of four fixed recall sections. Its backend fills the same struct memory.memory_candidates does and leaves confidence and use count at zero, because none of these statements selects them; the wire row omits both rather than carrying two fields that are always zero and would read as data. Archived and superseded memories are excluded, which the candidate loader does not do.

The typed maintenance.retryable_index_failures operation lists the memories whose indexing failed and is still worth retrying. Oldest failure first, so a caller working through the list makes progress rather than retrying the same head. A limit of zero adds no LIMIT clause, leaving the row bound as the only stop. Distinct memory identifiers come back, so a memory that failed several times appears once and the reply says nothing about how many attempts it has left.

The typed memory.list_session_scope_priority operation replaces the row reader. Two decisions are on the record with it. The ordering is DB2's, computed against DB2's own scope tables, so it stays behind the handler. And the scope the ordering depends on now travels in the request: the backend reads it from a thread-local that db2_memory_scope_context_set writes, which does not follow a call into another process.

The typed memory.list_session_scope_priority_like operation replaces the filtered variant of the priority list. The term is bound as a SQL LIKE pattern rather than a literal, so a wildcard the caller writes is significant and a caller sending a literal percent sign gets a wider result than it asked for -- that is on the record because the wire cannot show it. Identifiers cross and the scope travels, as for the unfiltered variant.

The typed memory.superseded_keys operation counts how many versions each key has. A version is not a column: it is a '#v' marker inside the key text, and this splits on the FIRST one -- so a key whose own text contains that marker before its version suffix is grouped under a base key that is not its own. Keys without the marker are absent entirely, so a key with exactly one version is indistinguishable here from one that was never versioned.

The typed memory.load_eval_corpus operation replaces the corpus loader. It tries three plans in order and the first to return a row wins, so the reply carries the label of the plan that answered: which corpus a caller got is not recoverable from the identifiers. Each plan carries its own LIMIT of 100, so the request limit bounds what is read back rather than what the plan selects. Identifiers cross; it is unscoped.

Private lookup inside the unit-graph rebuild: the value is read only to feed the rows that same rebuild is about to write, and is never returned to a caller. Exposing it would publish an intermediate of a composite operation as though it were an answer in its own right.

Private lookup inside the episode-relation rebuild: the value is read only to feed the rows that same rebuild is about to write, and is never returned to a caller. Exposing it would publish an intermediate of a composite operation as though it were an answer in its own right.

The typed memory.mark_merged_into operation points a session's low-confidence memories at the one that replaced them. It is a bulk write with no list of what it touched: the rows are chosen by session and confidence inside the statement, and the backend returns void, so a caller learns neither how many were merged nor that any were. A confidence ceiling that matches nothing and one that matches everything are the same acknowledgement.

The typed memory.negation_fts_search operation replaces the negation search. The tokens cross; joining them with OR and building the tsquery is the handler's, and so is the 1600-byte bound on the joined query, which truncates silently once the tokens exceed it. websearch_to_tsquery is used precisely because it does not syntax-error on arbitrary input. Identifiers cross and the scope travels, as for the other scoped searches.

The typed memory.negation_tokens_update operation replaces the extracted-token write, bounded to the extractor's own output width. The backend maps a null to an empty string and stores it, so an empty value is a request that clears the column rather than a malformed one.

The typed memory.pick_first_temporal_ref operation replaces the highest-ranked temporal reference lookup. The ordering is fixed policy inside the statement rather than a caller input, and a memory with no usable reference is reported as not_found since the backend succeeds only for a non-empty key.
The typed memory.expire operation wipes the L0 rows together with their provenance, so this half never runs alone and no partially expired L0 state is observable across the bus.
The typed memory.expire operation clears L0 provenance immediately before the rows it describes, inside one DB2 action that owns both halves.
The typed memory.expire operation applies each kind's own idle window from the private lifecycle thresholds, so the stale-L1 delete is never reachable with a caller-chosen kind or window.
The typed memory.expire operation clears stale-L1 provenance immediately before the rows it describes, under the same per-kind window and inside the same DB2 action.

The typed memory.demote operation cascades reduced confidence to dependants of the rows it just demoted, matched by the stamp it issued; exposing the cascade alone would let a caller match rows a different action had stamped.

The typed memory.demote_id operation replaces the single-row confidence decay; the multiplier and the floor below which a row stops decaying stay fixed policy behind the handler so a caller can only name which row decays, never how far.

The typed memory.demote operation applies each kind's own confidence floor and resistance-scaled idle window from the private lifecycle thresholds, so the per-kind demotion is never reachable with a caller-chosen threshold or window.

Enumerating the kinds present in a tier is a private pre-step of the tier-cycle operations; each one iterates the kinds it finds inside a single DB2 action rather than exposing a snapshot that can go stale between calls.

The typed memory.match_error_keys operation finds the memories whose key appears in an error message. The comparison puts the key on the pattern side of a LIKE, so a key containing a percent or an underscore is a wildcard: one such key matches text it has nothing to do with, and nothing escapes it. The scan reads every L1 and L2 memory above the confidence floor, so cost grows with the corpus, and the caller sees a truncated list and a full one the same way.

The typed memory.promote_stable operation applies the complete fixed stability policy — tier, kinds, confidence floor, use count, and settling window — so callers cannot promote rows into the slow-changing tier on terms of their own.

The typed memory.reclassify_directives operation fixes the tiers and directive kinds and carries only the approval gate, which is a genuine caller choice: the batch path runs ungated while the operator approval path requires a recorded approval for policies.

The typed memory.record_l4_approval operation fixes the approved tier and carries the bounded approver and note an operator supplies; DB2 owns the approval row that memory.reclassify_directives later reads under its gate. The approver defaults to operator only for a null argument, which the wire cannot send.

The typed memory.provenance_by_id operation reads where a memory came from. What it calls a version is the memory's updated_at stamp, which has one-second resolution, so two writes inside the same second produce the same version and a caller watching for change sees none. The backend separates a memory that is not there from a read that failed, and the reply carries that three-way rather than folding it into an empty answer.

Provenance cleanup is an internal compatibility step of the complete memory.delete operation; it must commit with canonical row, vector, relation, and derived-state deletion rather than cross the bus independently.
Provenance append is private bookkeeping inside complete insert, merge, consolidate, and supersede operations; no generic caller-controlled provenance mutation crosses the bus.

The typed memory.provenance_list operation lists what has happened to a memory. It is ordered oldest first, so a caller whose array fills keeps the earliest entries and loses the newest -- the opposite of what a reader asking what happened recently wants, and nothing says the tail was dropped. The row carries the memory identifier the caller already supplied, which is the only field of the six that tells it nothing.

The typed memory.prune_orphaned_l0 operation replaces the doctor-invoked retention delete for expired unlinked short-term rows; the tier and age window stay fixed policy behind the handler so no caller can widen the delete.

The typed memory.retro_scan_marker operation records that the retroactive contradiction scan ran. It writes the row memory.last_retro_scan finds by matching a free-text column against one particular word, so the two are joined by a convention rather than a column -- and this is the writer that has to keep it. The stamp is the caller's, not DB2's, so a caller with a wrong clock records a scan that appears to have run at the wrong time.

The typed memory.reject operation replaces the confidence penalty. The backend's reason parameter is discarded and never persisted, so the wire operation deliberately does not carry it rather than implying a rejection rationale is recorded; the penalty and floor stay fixed policy.

The typed memory.relation_dates operation lists the dates a memory's relations begin. Only relations whose start date is not empty are listed, so the count is not the memory's relation count and a caller cannot tell a memory with no relations from one whose relations are all undated. The date is a text column ordered as text, which is right for the one format DB2 writes and wrong for any other that reaches it.

The typed memory.relation_insert operation records a relation a memory asserts. The relation name is free text here -- unlike db2_fact_commit, which puts a relation through a gate before writing one -- so the same graph can hold a checked relation and an unchecked one under the same name. The backend returns void, so the acknowledgement cannot say the row landed.

Private first half of memory_refresh_episode_relations: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.relations_for_entity operation lists the relations an entity takes part in. Either end matches, and both are compared case-insensitively, so the reply's own source and target say which way each relation points rather than repeating the argument. The order is newest memory first, then heaviest, so the limit keeps the most recent rather than the strongest.

The typed memory.relations_search operation searches relations by substring across both endpoints, the relation name and the fact text. The query is wrapped in wildcards rather than matched as one, so a short query matches almost every row and the limit decides what a caller sees. Nothing escapes the query, so a percent or underscore in it widens the match further.

The typed memory.relations_search_as_of operation searches relations as they stood at an instant. A relation with an empty start stamp counts as valid before the instant and one with an empty end stamp as valid after it, so a relation with neither is returned for every instant -- absence reads as always rather than never. The stamps are compared as text, so a differently formatted instant compares wrongly rather than failing.

The typed memory.relations_supporting operation finds the relations that carry a stated fact about an entity. It differs from memory.relations_for_entity twice over: the token matches either endpoint as a substring rather than exactly, and a relation whose fact text is empty is skipped, because a relation with nothing written on it supports nothing.
The raw row insert is private implementation of a complete memory.insert operation, which must validate input, insert the canonical row, attach provenance and scope, and commit before replying.

The typed memory.scene_member_exists operation replaces the membership probe. The pair is matched in the order given, unlike memory.unit_edge_exists beside it which tries both orders, so swapping the arguments here asks a genuinely different question. A statement that cannot run answers false, indistinguishable from an absent membership.

The typed memory.scene_memberships operation lists the scenes a memory belongs to and how strongly. The statement has no ordering, so a memory in more scenes than the caller's array holds answers with an arbitrary subset -- and because the strength is what a caller would rank by, the rows it needs most are exactly the ones it may not receive.
Clearing thread-local memory query context has no wire representation; each bounded memory request carries its scope and DB2 discards that request-local state before replying.
Reading process thread-local scope is private memory-operation plumbing; explicit bounded scope fields replace implicit caller-owned state across the bus.
Per-candidate rank probes would expose chatty implicit state; DB2 applies scope ranking inside the complete bounded memory search and returns only the ranked result set.
A setter for thread-local workspace and project scope cannot cross a process boundary; typed memory requests carry the bounded scope with the operation that consumes it.
A single-row scope-tag SQL probe is private DB2 query planning; complete memory search and retrieval operations enforce scope before returning bounded rows.

The typed memory.scope_tag_insert operation tags a memory with a scope. Its statement does nothing on conflict, so tagging twice is a no-op rather than a duplicate -- which is right, and also invisible: the backend returns void, so a repeat and a first write are the same acknowledgement. The scope type is free text, and memory.scopes_list orders by a fixed preference over those types, so a type outside that list sorts last.

The typed memory.scopes_list operation lists the scopes a memory is tagged with. The rows come back in an order the statement fixes -- a CASE over the scope type -- so a caller reading the first row is reading whichever type that expression ranks highest, not the one the memory was tagged with first. Truncation at the caller's array therefore drops the lowest-ranked types rather than an arbitrary set, and says nothing about having done so.

The typed memory.search_by_pattern operation searches the two session-facing tiers by pattern. The pattern reaches LIKE as written, so a caller sending text that happens to contain an underscore or a percent sign is searching for something wider than it typed -- and neither the backend nor this boundary escapes them. Only the L1 and L2 tiers are searched, so a memory promoted past them is unreachable here however well it matches.

The typed memory.search_facts_patterns_by_keyword operation replaces the keyword search. Which tiers and kinds count as a fact or a pattern is DB2 policy and stays behind the handler. Its statement did not select the identifier, so every row came back with id zero: a caller serialising the row published a zero identifier and resolved no headline. The identifier is selected now, which is also what makes the operation expressible as an identifier list. Scope and reply shape follow the other scoped searches.

The typed memory.session_memories operation lists the memories a session wrote, oldest first. That order means the limit keeps the beginning of a session and discards its end, which is the opposite of what most listings here do and of what a caller asking for recent context would expect. Every tier is included.
Listing a session's L0 rows is a private step of the future memory.session_fold operation; exposing the list separately would race the L1 checkpoint insert and subsequent provenance-aware purge.

Purging a session's L0 memories and provenance is a private mutation inside the future memory.session_fold transaction; it cannot be an independent wire operation without risking loss between checkpoint creation and deletion.

The typed memory.session_neighbors_after operation replaces the forward walk. It is the mirror of session_neighbors_before and shares its format; the difference is the comparison and the direction, which the two policies state. An anchor of zero selects the whole session from its first memory here rather than nothing, which is the one place the two operations answer a caller's zero differently.

The typed memory.session_neighbors_before operation replaces the backward walk. It returns identifiers for the reason top_l2_facts records. It is not session-scoped in the sense the scoped reads are: the session identifier in the request is the filter itself, not the ranking context, so no scope triple travels with it. An anchor of zero selects nothing, which is a property of the comparison rather than an error, and is recorded because the reply cannot distinguish it from a session with no earlier memories.

The typed memory.set_artifact operation attaches an artifact to a memory. Unlike most writes here it counts the rows its update matched, so a memory that does not exist is reported unchanged rather than acknowledged -- the reply means what it says. An empty hash is stored as a null rather than an empty string, so a caller reading the column back cannot use the same test for 'not sent' as for every other text column on the row.

The typed memory.set_cognified_kind operation replaces the cognified-kind write, bounded to the memory record's own kind width. The backend refuses an empty kind and returns void, so the wire refuses it too and acknowledges rather than inventing a count.

The typed memory.set_source_session operation replaces the session attribution write, bounded to the memory record's own session width. The backend accepts an empty session, which clears the column, so the wire carries a zero minimum rather than borrowing the non-empty minimum of the neighbouring setters.
Setting replacement validity is an internal post-insert step of the future composite memory.supersede transaction and cannot be exposed as a separately committed caller mutation.
Renaming and closing the prior row is an internal step of the future composite memory.supersede transaction; callers cannot safely sequence this mutation across the event bus.

The typed memory.stats_counts operation returns the complete tier, kind, and conflict breakdown of the canonical relational corpus; the host layers its own PageRank timings on top and DB2 owns none of those.

Private first half of the summary refresh: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.summaries_list operation lists a memory's summaries, oldest first. It takes both a limit and an array size, and the two are separate bounds: the statement applies the limit, the loop applies the array, and a caller passing a limit larger than its array gets the array. A limit of zero is not none -- the backend substitutes its own default -- so the only way to ask for nothing is not to ask.

The typed memory.summarise_clusters operation finds sessions holding enough low-confidence facts to be worth summarising. Four conditions are written into the statement rather than the request -- the tier, the kind, that the memory is not already merged, and that the confidence is at or below what was asked -- so a caller can move only the last of them. The average returned is over the same rows the count counted, which makes it an average of the low-confidence facts rather than of the session.

Private second half of memory_refresh_summaries: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

The typed memory.temporal_insert operation records a time reference a memory carries. The granularity is free text that nothing checks, and memory.temporal_refs_list returns it as stored -- so what a reference means is the writer's word at both ends. The backend returns void, so the acknowledgement cannot say the row landed, and nothing deduplicates, so the same reference twice is two rows.

Private first half of the temporal-reference refresh: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.temporal_refs_list operation lists the time references a memory carries, heaviest first and then by insertion. That second key makes the order total, so two references of equal weight come back the same way every time -- which most lists here do not guarantee. The granularity is a free-text column, so what a reference means is the writer's word rather than a checked vocabulary.

The typed memory.top_l2_facts operation replaces the row reader. It returns identifiers rather than rows, because the generated client sizes its reply buffer as a local array and sixty-four memory rows do not belong on a caller's stack; the caller reattaches content through memory.get_content. The session scope travels in the request for the same reason as list_session_scope_priority.

The typed memory.touch operation replaces the retrieval-accounting bump; the increment and the stamp are fixed policy behind the handler so a caller can record that a memory was used but cannot choose by how much or when.

The typed memory.unit_active_meta operation reads a memory unit's weight and kind. The unit is only visible while its memory sits in one of three tiers, so a unit that exists answers as absent once its memory moves out of them, and the reply cannot say which of the two happened. The three tiers are written into the statement rather than passed, so a caller cannot ask about a unit whose memory is anywhere else.

The typed memory.unit_edge_exists operation replaces the edge probe. Both orders are tried, so an edge stored either way answers true and the arguments are interchangeable -- the opposite of memory.scene_member_exists beside it, and not visible in a Boolean. The edge type is ignored, and nothing stops the same pair being stored twice, so this answers whether the units are connected at all and never how.

Private second half of memory_refresh_units_graph: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

Private first half of memory_refresh_units_graph: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.episode_card_insert operation records an episode card for a memory. The backend returns void, so the acknowledgement says the call was made. Nothing deduplicates the key, so the same card written twice is two rows, and memory.unit_first_episode_card_id -- which takes the first -- then depends on which of the two the database returns first.

The typed memory.first_episode_card operation finds a memory's first episode card. First means the lowest identifier, so it is the first written rather than the first by any property of the card -- and because memory.episode_card_insert deduplicates nothing, writing the same card twice makes the earlier duplicate the answer forever. Zero means no card, which is also what a failed read returns.

Private second half of memory_refresh_units_graph: the derived rows cleared by the matching *_delete_for_memory call are recomputed and reinserted here. The delete and the reinserts are one rebuild, so exposing either half would let a caller run half of it and would split the rebuild across the process boundary. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates.

The typed memory.unit_ids_for_memory operation lists the units a memory was split into. The statement has no ORDER BY, so the order is whatever Postgres returns and is not stable between calls -- anything pairing this list with another by position is relying on something nobody promised. A memory that does not exist and one with no units both answer with nothing.

Private first half of memory_refresh_units_graph: the derived rows are cleared and then immediately recomputed and reinserted. Exposing the delete on its own would offer a capability no caller wants and would split the rebuild across the process boundary, so a failure between the delete and the reinserts would leave the memory stripped of its derived rows. The composite refresh is the operation that migrates; this half never runs alone.

The typed memory.units_list operation lists a memory's units. The statement has no ordering, so a memory with more units than the caller's array holds answers with whichever ones the database returned first -- and which ones those are is not decided by anything. Every other list over a memory's parts here orders by weight or by id; this one does not, so it is the one whose truncation cannot be reasoned about.

The typed memory.update_content operation replaces the canonical text rewrite, bounded to the memory record's own content width; the row is DB2 authority and re-deriving any vector from the new text is a separate provider concern.

The typed memory.valid_at operation preserves the backend's three-way answer: in force, not in force, or could not be evaluated. The third is carried as invalid_state rather than folded into a negative verdict, because an unevaluated comparison is not the same claim as one that came back false.
The legacy-workspace membership probe remains an internal compatibility predicate folded into scoped memory operations, not a separately callable bus capability.

The typed memory.workspace_tag_insert operation replaces the workspace attribution insert, bounded to DB2's own workspace identifier width. The backend returns void and its statement is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the acknowledgement carries no count: a repeat is a no-op rather than a failure and there is nothing to report either way.

The typed maintenance.mining_job_complete operation records that a mining job ran. The high-water mark only moves forward -- a lower one sent is discarded silently, so a job re-run over earlier data cannot say so. The error is written unconditionally, so completing without one erases the last failure and the job reads as though it never failed. Nothing checks a row matched, so completing a job that does not exist is acknowledged.

The typed maintenance.mining_job_get operation reads one mining job's schedule and last outcome. The identifier is a name the caller chose rather than one the database assigned, so two callers using the same name share a job without either learning of the other. The last error is the last one recorded, not the last one that mattered: a successful run overwrites it with an empty string, so a job that has failed and then succeeded looks like one that never failed.

The typed maintenance.mining_job_try_lock operation replaces the advisory lock. It is keyed by a hash of the job identifier rather than the identifier, so two different jobs can collide on one lock and the second will be refused as though its own job were already running. That is a property of the backend, not of this boundary, and it is recorded here because the Boolean cannot show it.

The typed learning.mining_seed_job_defaults operation registers the mining jobs and their schedules on first run. The job list and intervals are fixed policy, and so is the do-nothing conflict rule: it is what keeps a seed pass from overwriting an interval an operator has since tuned. This operation reports success or failure and no count, because the number it could report would be the seeds attempted rather than the rows created.

The typed organization.ontology_approve operation approves a proposed relationship type. The name is normalized before anything is matched, so two spellings can reach the same type. Promoting the type to active is best-effort and its result is discarded -- a seeded type is already active -- while marking the evaluation approved must match exactly one row or the whole transaction rolls back. So a refusal means there was no evaluation to approve, never that the type failed to be promoted.

The typed memory.ontology_eval_count operation reads how often a relation type has been seen. The type is normalised before the lookup, so two spellings of the same relation answer as one and a caller cannot tell which spelling the stored row used. A relation type that normalises to nothing is refused the same way a failed read is, and the reply carries the found flag the backend's single negative return value could not.

The typed organization.ontology_eval_status operation replaces the evaluation status read. A relation type that has never been evaluated reads back as the empty string, and because no recorded status is empty, that is a usable signal rather than an ambiguity -- unlike the other string reads in this batch, which is why it is worth stating the difference.

The typed organization.ontology_map operation maps a proposed relationship type onto an existing one. It is the strictest of the three ontology decisions: both names are normalized, the target must already resolve to a real type, and a type cannot be mapped to itself -- which two differently written names can become after normalization. As with approve and reject the evaluation must match exactly one row, and marking the source type mapped is the best-effort half of the transaction.

The typed organization.ontology_reject operation rejects a proposed relationship type. It writes the same two rows as organization.ontology_approve in the opposite order: the evaluation must match exactly one row first, and marking the type rejected is the best-effort half. Both run in one transaction, so a refusal leaves neither row changed, and as with approve a refusal only ever means there was no evaluation to decide.
The typed lifecycle.postgres_status operation replaces the doctor command's direct PostgreSQL diagnostics call with bounded availability and metric fields.
The typed lifecycle.pool_status operation replaces the production health caller; PostgreSQL pool occupancy and counters remain DB2 process authority.

The injected embedder callback is a process-local compatibility seam and cannot cross the bus; callers resolve the running endpoint's dimension before submitting the typed reset operation, which always carries an explicit target.

The typed memory.prospective_counts operation counts prospective memories by state. The backend returns nothing -- it is a void function -- so a database it could not reach is four zeros and an empty table is four zeros, and the reply cannot separate them. It names four states and drops every other group, so the four need not add up to the table. There is no scope: this is every prospective memory the installation holds.

The typed memory.prospective_list operation lists prospective memories in a state. An empty state is not an empty result: it drops the condition and lists every one of them, which is a different query rather than a wider one. The order is newest first with the identifier breaking ties, so a caller paging by limit alone re-reads the same head each time.

The typed memory.prospective_list_armed operation lists every armed prospective memory. Its statement carries no limit at all, unlike the four listings beside it, so the wire's row bound is the only thing that stops the read and a caller cannot tell a list cut there from one that ended.

The typed memory.prospective_by_entity operation finds the armed prospective memories anchored to an entity. The comparison lowers the stored anchor and not the argument, so a caller that sends a name as written matches nothing -- the field is named for what it expects. Only armed memories match, so one already triggered is invisible here whatever its anchor.

The typed memory.prospective_by_file operation finds the armed prospective memories anchored to a file. The path is compared exactly, where the entity listing beside it compares a lowered anchor, so the two differ in a way neither name nor reply shows. Only armed memories match.

The typed memory.prospective_by_trigger_terms operation finds the armed prospective memories whose trigger text matches a turn. The turn becomes a full-text query and the trigger is stemmed as English, so matching is about word stems rather than the words as written, and a trigger in another language matches differently than its author would expect.

The typed memory.prospective_set_state operation replaces the state write. The state is stored unchecked and the update stamp is DB2's clock rather than the caller's, so a caller records that something changed but never claims when. An identifier naming no prospective memory updates nothing and is acknowledged.

The typed maintenance.prospective_sweep_expired operation replaces the sweep that retires armed prospective memories whose validity window has closed. The two states it moves between, and the requirement that a row carry a validity window at all, are fixed policy: a caller able to choose them could expire memories that were never given an expiry. The comparison is made against the database clock rather than a caller-supplied instant, so a wrong clock on one caller cannot retire memories early.
The typed lifecycle.reembed_clear_maintenance operation keeps the dimension-consistency check, optional force override, diagnostic snapshot, and marker delete inside one DB2 action.
The typed lifecycle.reembed_clear operation replaces the curator drain's direct maintenance-marker delete with an idempotent DB2 mutation.
The typed lifecycle.reembed_status operation replaces direct reads of the canonical maintenance marker while retaining DB2 schema and rebuild authority.

The typed organization.rel_types_ensure_seed operation persists the relation-type ontology on first run. What it can pin is only the persistence rule -- active status and do-nothing conflicts -- because the seed set itself is declared by the ontology module outside DB2. The catalog records that boundary rather than copying a table it does not own and would then have to keep in step.

The typed learning.rules_decay operation replaces the pass that ages rule weights and archives the ones that fall through the floor. Every constant is fixed policy: a caller able to send the decay amount or the intervals could age a hard directive out in a single call, and one able to send the archive threshold could delete rules that are still in force.

The typed learning.rules_delete_by_id operation replaces the rule deletion. Its backend reports whether a row was removed, so the reply carries that: an identifier naming no rule is distinguishable from a deletion that happened, which most of the writes in this batch cannot manage.

The typed learning.rules_delete_by_directive_type operation deletes every rule carrying a directive type -- unlike learning.rules_delete_by_id beside it, one call can remove an unbounded number of rules, and the reply's count is the only record of how many. The rules cache it drops afterwards is a static inside the module process, but it is keyed on a signature read from the rules table, so another process notices the deletion on its next read regardless.

The typed learning.rules_find_by_title operation finds a rule by its title, matched without regard to case. learning.rules_insert applies no such test when writing, so two rules whose titles differ only in case both exist and this answers with whichever the database returns first -- there is no ordering and no limit. learning.feedback_record reinforces through this same lookup, so it reinforces an arbitrary one of them.

The typed learning.rules_insert operation writes a rule. Nothing deduplicates the title, and learning.rules_find_by_title matches titles without regard to case, so this is the write that creates the ambiguity that read then resolves arbitrarily. The weight is stored as sent: learning.feedback_record, writing to the same table, caps it at a hundred, and this does not, so the ceiling depends on which path a rule arrived through. An empty polarity becomes positive.

The typed learning.rules_list operation lists every rule, heaviest first and then by title. Its statement carries no limit, so the wire's row bound is the only thing that stops it and a caller cannot tell a list cut there from one that ended. An expired rule is listed like any other: the expiry stamp comes back but nothing here filters on it.

The typed learning.rules_list_by_tier operation lists the rules at or above a weight. The floor is inclusive, and a floor of zero makes it learning.rules_list -- same order, same absent limit, same treatment of expired rules. A caller cannot ask for a tier and a limit at once; the row bound is still the only stop.

The typed learning.rules_list_hard operation lists the rules typed hard. The type is matched as that literal string, so a rule typed anything else is absent however heavy it is -- weight and hardness are separate here, which the shared ordering by weight hides. Like the two listings beside it, nothing limits the statement.

The typed learning.rules_reinforce_directive operation sets a rule's directive type and stamps it reinforced, optionally setting its weight. The backend decides whether to set the weight from the sign of the argument, and a negative number is not something this envelope can carry, so the request says so in a flag of its own instead. Nothing checks a row matched. Unlike learning.rules_update_directive_type this does touch updated_at, so the two writes leave the same column in different states.

Names the tier a rule weight falls in. Three comparisons against two constants, no store -- the weight already crossed the boundary on the rule row, and naming its band is arithmetic the reader of that row can do.

The typed learning.rules_update_directive_type operation sets how binding a rule is. The header names three values -- hard, soft and session -- and nothing enforces them, so a fourth is stored and read back. Nothing checks a row matched, so setting the type of a rule that does not exist is acknowledged. The row's updated_at is not touched, so a rule whose bindingness changed looks unmodified to anything watching that column.
The configured model identity is injected into the DB2 owner before initialization; exposing a post-attachment setter would violate atomic activation.
The operator-pinned embedding width is private pre-initialization configuration; the bus exposes only the resolved effective dimension.
The descriptor-owned default width is injected during private module bootstrap and is immutable once the DB2 process attaches.
Pin precedence is private startup configuration consumed while DB2 establishes canonical schema authority; it is not a runtime mutation.
Pool capacity is fixed before DB2 initialization and remains private to the process owner; lifecycle.pool_status exposes the resulting bounded state.
Schema apply-versus-verify mode is a private bootstrap choice made before opening DB2 and cannot be changed through the serving bus.
Connection and pool teardown belongs to supervised process termination; callers cannot remotely shut down the required DB2 capability.

The typed index.minhash_delete_file operation drops one file's minhash signature in the project's current generation. Unlike index.minhash_delete_current_generation beside it, which deletes signatures and their LSH buckets together, this deletes only the signature and leaves every bucket entry the file put in the index. Anything reading the buckets still finds the file until the whole generation is cleared.

The typed index.minhash_delete_current_generation operation drops a project's minhash signatures and the LSH buckets built from them. The two deletes run one after the other with no transaction around them, so a failure between them leaves the signatures gone and the buckets pointing at nothing, and the reply reports only that the second statement failed. Recorded because the pair reads as one operation and is not one.

The typed maintenance.synth_enqueue operation replaces the queue insert. Its column references artifacts, so an artifact that does not exist is refused by the database -- and because this operation has one result, that refusal reaches the caller as an internal failure rather than as something it can act on. Enqueuing one already queued does nothing and is acknowledged, so a repeat is indistinguishable from a new job.

The typed maintenance.synth_mark_done operation replaces the completion update. Marking something already done, or never queued at all, updates nothing and is acknowledged just the same; the reply says the statement ran, not that it changed anything.

The typed maintenance.synth_mark_failed operation replaces the synthesis failure write. It is the mirror of evidence_mark_failed against the other queue, and shares its property: the attempt count is the statement's, not the caller's.

The typed maintenance.synth_reenqueue_all operation replaces the reset that requeues every learning synthesis operation after a learning version change. Its reach and its discard are identical to the evidence reset already on the bus: no predicate, attempts back to zero, last error cleared. Both are triggered by the same version bump and both are recorded as fixed policy, so the pair cannot drift apart without the gate noticing.

The typed organization.task_add_edge operation links one task to another. Unlike memory.memory_link_create beside it, which does the same thing for memories, nothing deduplicates here: adding the same edge twice stores it twice, and organization.task_edges then returns it twice. The relation is stored unchecked, so an unknown relation is recorded rather than refused.

The typed organization.task_create operation creates a task. Nothing checks the parent exists -- the column carries no foreign key here -- so a task can be created beneath a parent that is not there and nothing later says its tree is broken. The state and confidence are fixed in the statement at todo and one, so a caller cannot create a task in any other state. The stamps are DB2's clock.

The typed organization.task_delete operation removes a task and its edges. It runs two statements with no transaction and ignores whether the edge delete succeeded, so a caller can be told the task is gone while its edges remain. The schema's foreign key cascades the edges anyway, which is why the explicit delete looked safe to ignore; the catalog records that the pair is not atomic instead of leaving that reasoning in a comment.

The typed organization.task_get operation reads one task. The identifier carries no scope, so a caller holding a number reads whichever session's task it names -- the session is returned rather than checked. A parent identifier of zero means no parent, and a non-zero one is returned whether or not that task exists, because organization.task_create never checked. A task that is not there and a read that failed are both a zero flag.

The typed organization.task_edges operation lists the edges touching a task. The task may be either end, so the reply's own source and target say which way each edge points. Nothing orders the result, so which edges survive the limit is whatever the database returned first, and a task with no edges and a task that does not exist both answer with nothing.

The typed organization.task_subtasks operation lists a task's immediate children, oldest first. Only one level: a grandchild is not here, so a caller walking a tree has to call again per level and cannot tell a leaf from a task that does not exist. The order is by creation, unlike organization.task_list beside it, which leads with the most recently updated.

The typed organization.task_list operation lists tasks by state and session. Each filter is dropped when empty rather than matched against the empty string, so sending neither lists every task -- four statements behind one name. The order is by most recently updated, so a task touched by anything moves to the head whatever its state.

The typed organization.task_update_state operation replaces the task state write. Unlike the other state writes in this batch its backend distinguishes an update that matched no row from one that did, so the reply carries that rather than a bare acknowledgement -- a caller can tell that the task it named does not exist, which the others cannot.
A caller-held tenant transaction cannot cross the bus; each tenancy or tenant-scoped operation carries bounded verifier-owned principal fields and owns context setup through completion.
Committing caller-owned tenant state is not a wire operation; a complete scoped DB2 request commits before its reply and never returns a transaction token.
Rollback and tenant-GUC clearing remain DB2 process cleanup; failures, cancellation, and denied scope roll back before the typed operation returns.

The typed organization.tool_registry_lookup operation reads a registered tool's input schema and side-effect class. A name nobody registered is not an error -- the backend returns success with nothing filled in -- so the found flag is the only thing separating an unregistered tool from a registered one, and a read that failed returns the same. A registered tool with an empty side-effect column is read as 'read', which is the least dangerous of the classes.

The typed learning.trace_mining_last_id operation reads the high-water mark the next mining pass resumes from. A never-mined corpus and a failed read are both zero, and the consequence is worth naming: a zero sends the next pass back to the beginning, so a read failure costs a full rescan rather than losing anything. That is recorded because it makes the collapse cheap in one direction and expensive in the other.

The typed learning.trace_mining_record operation replaces the watermark write. Each call appends a row stamped with DB2's own clock rather than updating one, so it is declared unsafe to replay: a second call does not restore the state the first found, it adds to it. The stamp is DB2's and never crosses.

The typed memory.typed_fact_recall operation recalls the facts asserted about a subject. Only active facts are returned, so a retracted one is absent rather than marked. An empty relation is not an empty result: it drops the condition, and it also changes the order -- by relation then identifier when unfiltered, by identifier alone when filtered -- so the two forms are not the same query narrowed.

Commits or rolls back a transaction the caller began earlier through a separate call. A transaction cannot span bus calls: the caller holds no connection, and the module has no way to know which caller's work a later commit refers to. Startup work that must be atomic belongs in one operation that owns its whole transaction.
Destroys the caller-held runtime object opened above, including its mutex. It operates entirely on memory the caller owns and has nothing to send.

Opens a caller-held runtime object: a struct carrying a pthread mutex and its own Postgres connection, both created for and owned by the calling process. Neither can be represented on the wire, for the same reason db2_conn cannot. A caller needing operator status across the boundary needs an operation that returns the status, not one that hands back a handle.

Reads status through the caller-held runtime under its mutex, sampling twice and comparing to reject a torn read. Both the lock and the retry are properties of holding the object locally; across a bus the caller holds nothing to lock, so this stays private and a status operation would have to own that sampling itself.
A memcmp of two caller-owned structs. It reads nothing and belongs to whoever holds the snapshots; sending two structures across a boundary to be compared would cost more than the comparison.

The typed maintenance.vector_index_op_record operation records whether a vector write landed. The backend returns nothing at all, so this reply says the call arrived and cannot say the row did -- the bookkeeping that exists to notice failed writes cannot itself report failing. Recording the same point again counts an attempt rather than replacing one, which is what lets the retry sweep give up. A successful record stamps the index time; a failed one leaves it null.

The typed maintenance.vector_index_op_remove operation forgets a vector point's bookkeeping once the point itself is gone. The backend returns nothing, so this reply is a receipt for the call and not for the delete -- a caller cannot learn whether a row was there. That is tolerable only because absence is the intended end state either way: removing a point with no row is a success, so a lost delete shows up as a retry row that never clears rather than as anything unsafe.

This reads a process configuration flag and issues no statement: it reports whether DB2 was started ephemeral. On the bus it would let one process ask another about its startup configuration, which is not a fact DB2 owns on the caller's behalf. A caller that needs it is asking about its own runtime and should read its own configuration.

The typed maintenance.witness_checkpoint_anchor_coverage operation counts retained checkpoints signed by a key id other than the one the caller can verify with -- evidence a key-holding kb cannot check, which must stop startup. The key id is sixteen raw bytes and the envelope has no byte field, so it crosses as thirty-two hex characters and is decoded here; a malformed one is refused rather than truncated. coverage_read is carried because could-not-verify is not verified.

The typed maintenance.witness_checkpoint_freshness operation reports how many checkpoints exist and how old the newest is. The release gate closes on a chain that has stalled, because a local rewrite stops being caught once signed-root production stops -- but a kb with no checkpoints has not stalled, it has no evidence yet, so zero is deliberately not stale. That makes carrying freshness_read necessary: the caller must fail closed on a read that did not happen, which otherwise arrives as the same zero.

The typed learning.workflow_pattern_insert operation records a workflow pattern. Nothing deduplicates the pattern text, so the same pattern learned twice becomes two rows. The confidence is stored as sent and nothing bounds it to a probability. The backend fills its output struct from the arguments rather than reading the row back, so a caller that trusted that struct was told what it sent -- which is why this operation answers with the identifier alone.

Fills a maintenance configuration struct with its default values. It reads nothing and writes nothing: the defaults are constants in the source. A caller needs them before it can decide what to ask for, which is the wrong side of a request to be answering.

The typed maintenance.memory_lint operation reports what is wrong with the memory store. Three checks -- orphans, concept gaps, stale references -- fill one list in that order and each stops at the bound, so a full list does not mean those are the worst problems, it means the later checks never ran. The issue type is the only thing saying which check produced a row.

Answers whether a string is a well-formed metric name, by length and character class. Validation the caller must do before it sends anything, so making it a round trip would put the check after the request it is meant to gate.

Renders metric rows as a Prometheus exposition. The rows come from the organization.metrics_snapshot read; this turns them into text. Formatting rows a caller already holds is not a question about the store, and sending them back to be formatted would double the bytes for no answer that is not already there.
Hashes a string to hex. Nothing about it is DB2; it lives here because the telemetry token check needed a digest and this is where that check is. It stays linked.

Compares two hex digests in constant time. Sending it over a bus would cost the property it exists for -- the comparison would still be constant-time, and the round trip around it would not be, so the timing it hides would reappear at the boundary. It must stay a linked call.
